# Bioremediation, biogas

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Bioremediation** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Microbes in Human Welfare fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Bioremediation
### biogas

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

Microbes can be put to work on our waste. **Bioremediation** uses microorganisms to break pollutants down into harmless substances — oil-eating bacteria (*Pseudomonas*) after spills, microbes cleaning sewage in treatment plants. **Biogas** is the fuel side of the same idea: anaerobic methanogen bacteria digest animal dung and plant waste and release methane-rich gas for cooking and lighting.

**Concept flow — waste in, energy and clean water out (study in this order)**

| Step | Concept | Key organism / part |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sewage treatment — aerobic stage | Floc of bacteria and fungi in the aeration tank eats organic matter |
| 2 | Sewage treatment — anaerobic stage | Sludge digested by anaerobic bacteria; methane released |
| 3 | Bioremediation of oil spills | Pseudomonas putida and marine bacteria digest hydrocarbons |
| 4 | Biogas production | Methanogens (e.g. Methanobacterium) under anaerobic conditions |
| 5 | Biogas composition | ~50–70% methane + CO2 + traces; burns without smoke |
| 6 | By-product | Spent slurry = excellent nitrogen-rich fertiliser |

**Bioremediation and biogas — classified summary**

| Application | Microbe | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sewage treatment (aerobic) | Mixed bacterial-fungal floc | Waste water organic matter | Cleaner water + microbial floc |
| Sludge digestion (anaerobic) | Anaerobic bacteria + methanogens | Settled sludge | Methane + stabilised sludge |
| Oil-spill cleanup | Pseudomonas putida and marine hydrocarbon degraders | Petroleum hydrocarbons | CO2 + water + biomass |
| Biogas plant (gobar gas) | Methanobacterium (methanogen) | Cattle dung + water, anaerobic | Biogas (CH4-rich) + fertiliser slurry |
| Key condition | Methanogens are strict anaerobes | Sealed, oxygen-free digester | — |

**Parts of a floating-dome biogas plant and their jobs**

| Part | Job |
|---|---|
| Mixing tank / inlet | Dung + water slurry enters here |
| Digester (well) | Sealed underground tank where anaerobic digestion happens |
| Floating gas holder dome | Rises as gas collects; keeps constant pressure |
| Gas outlet pipe | Carries biogas to the kitchen / lamp |
| Overflow / sludge outlet | Spent slurry exits — used as fertiliser |
| Why the dome floats | It moves up and down with gas volume, so supply pressure stays steady |

## 5. Worked examples and applications

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example — why the digester must be airtight.** Methanogens are **obligate anaerobes**: oxygen poisons them. A cracked dome lets air in, the methane producers stop, acid-formers take over, and gas output collapses while the slurry turns sour. The floating dome is not decoration — it seals the digester while letting gas volume change. This single fact explains the whole engineering of the plant.

**Most-asked points (NEB).** (1) Define bioremediation with one example (oil-eating Pseudomonas). (2) Name the methanogen and state why anaerobic conditions are essential. (3) Give the composition of biogas and its two products (gas + slurry fertiliser). (4) Draw and label the floating-dome plant. (5) Name the two stages of sewage treatment and the role of the floc.

The binding condition is anaerobiosis. **Self-check:** can you label the six parts of the biogas plant and explain why the dome floats?

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Bioremediation: microbes degrade pollutants — Pseudomonas putida (oil spills, 'superbugs'), bacteria clean sewage in secondary treatment; the definition + example pair.
Trick 2: Biogas: anaerobic digestion — methanogens (Methanobacterium) in cow dung produce CH4 (~55–60%), CO2, H2S; gobar gas plant: mixing tank → digester → gas holder.
Trick 3: Methanogens are ANAEROBES — that is why the digester is sealed; cow dung inoculates the culture — the two conditions.
Trick 4: Uses of biogas: cooking, lighting; sludge residue = fertiliser — the dual product line.
